headline: High: agentic-flow can modify git and use MCP while argo-workflows can orchestrate API-driven jobs, creating default-pathway risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, so it may ingest external content; agent_b exposes REST/GRPC workflow inputs and handles artifacts/parameters. No shared channel is documented, but if agent_a’s outputs are routed into agent_b inputs, prompt-like content could be treated as instructions. Uncertainty keeps this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs are forwarded into agent_b workflow parameters without sanitization
IF a shared MCP or API bridge is configured between the pair
mitigations: Add an allowlist filter for agent_a outputs before passing them to agent_b
Require explicit human review of any text that becomes a workflow parameter
Disable MCP routing for untrusted content
Log and diff all cross-agent payloads for prompt-like directives

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and secrets (Ed25519 signatures), while agent_b processes artifacts and parameters. Both have allowlisted egress, so if shared workspace data flows from agent_a into agent_b, sensitive material can be exposed. The pairwise workspace is undocumented, so uncertainty escalates to medium.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem or artifact store
IF sensitive prompts or repository metadata are copied into agent_b inputs
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Redact secrets before any handoff
Restrict agent_b inputs to non-sensitive artifacts
Turn off cross-agent file sharing unless audited

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b is a workflow engine that can also act on shared artifacts and parameters. If both write to the same repo or artifact directory, conflicts are plausible even without explicit locking. No locking mechanism is documented, so choose medium over low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git checkout or artifact directory
IF workflow steps mutate shared parameters without coordination
mitigations: Assign separate write paths per agent
Serialize writes with a lock file or queue
Make agent_b consume immutable snapshots only
Disable git mutation in agent_a for shared repos

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis and modify repositories, while agent_b can orchestrate downstream workflow actions over artifacts and parameters. If agent_b treats agent_a’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into repeated workflow actions or bad commits. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is risky in default-style pipelines.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without validation
IF agent_a output is used to trigger workflow actions or commits
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require schema checks on agent_a outputs
Use human approval for any action-taking workflow
Limit agent_b to read-only evaluation of agent_a results

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. agent_a handles secrets and repository metadata, while agent_b handles artifacts and parameters, but there is no evidence of regulated data classes or cross-border processing. The other agent is cited because the compliance question is pairwise, though no breach is shown.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into the pair
IF one agent’s retention policy differs from the other’s on the same dataset
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Route sensitive workloads to a compliant environment
Review vendor residency and DPA status before deployment
